notes.text: The stones for his pillow, and the heavens for his canopy! Yet his comfort in the divine blessing, and his confidence in the divine protection, made him easy, even when he lay thus exposed: being sure that his God made him to dwell in safety, he could lie down and sleep upon a stone.

Behold a ladder set upon the earth, and the top of it reached heaven, the angels ascending and descending on it, and the Lord stood above it — This might represent

1. The providence of God, by which there is a constant correspondence kept up between heaven and earth. The counsels of heaven are executed on earth, and the affairs of this earth are all known in heaven. Providence doth his work gradually and by steps; angels are employed as ministering spirits to serve all the designs of providence, and the wisdom of God is at the upper end of the ladder, directing all the motions of second causes to his glory. The angels are active spirits, continually ascending and descending; they rest not day nor night. They ascend to give account of what they have done, and to receive orders; and desend to execute the orders they have received. This vision gave seasonable comfort to Jacob, letting him know that he had both a good guide and good guard; that though he was to wander from his father's house, yet he was the care of Providence, and the charge of the holy angels.

2. The mediation of Christ. He is this ladder: the foot on earth in his human nature, the top in heaven in his divine nature; or the former is his humiliation, the latter is his exaltation. All the intercourse between heaven and earth since the fall is by this ladder. Christ is the way: all God's favours come to us, and all our services come to him, by Christ. If God dwell with us, and we with him, it is by Christ: we have no way of getting to heaven but by this ladder; for the kind offices the angels do us, are all owing to Christ, who hath reconciled things on earth and things in heaven, Colossians i, 20.

In thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed — Christ is the great blessing of the world: all that are blessed, whatever family they are of, are blessed in him, and none of any family are excluded from blessedness in him, but those that exclude themselves.

Behold I am with thee — Wherever we are, we are safe, if we have God's favourable presence with us. He knew not, but God foresaw what hardships he would meet with in his uncle's service, and therefore promiseth to preserve him in all places. God knows how to give his people graces and comforts accommodated to the events that shall be, as well as to those that are. He was now going as an exile into a place far distant, but God promiseth him to bring him again to this land. He seemed to be forsaken of all his friends, but God gives him this assurance, I will not leave thee.

Surely the Lord is in this place, and I knew it not — God's manifestations of himself to his people carry their own evidence along with them. God can give undeniable demonstrations of his presence, such as give abundant satisfaction to the souls of the faithful, that God is with them of a truth; satisfaction not communicable to others, but convincing to themselves. We sometimes meet with God there, where we little thought of meeting with him. He is there where we did not think he had been, is found there where we asked not for him.

He was afraid — So far was he from being puffed up. The more we see of God, the more cause we see for holy trembling and blushing before him. Those whom God is pleased to manifest himself to, are laid and kept very low in their own eyes, and see cause to fear even the Lord and his goodness, Hosea iii, 5. And said, How dreadful is this place! - That is, the appearance of God in this place is to be thought of, but with a holy awe and reverence; I shall have a respect for this place, and remember it by this token as long as I live. Not that he thought the place itself any nearer the divine visions than any other places; but what he saw there at this time was, as it were, the house of God, the residence of the Divine Majesty, and the gate of heaven, that is, the general rendezvous of the inhabitants of the upper world; as the meetings of a city were in their gates; or, the angels ascending and descending were like travelers passing and repassing through the gates of a city.

He set up the stone for a pillar — To mark the place again, if he came back, and erect a lasting monument of God's favour to him: and because he had not time now to build an altar here, as Abraham did in the places where God appeared to him, chap. xii, 7, he therefore poured oil on the top of this stone, which probably was the ceremony then used in dedicating their altars, as an earnest of his building an altar when he should have conveniencies for it, as afterwards he did, in gratitude to God, chap. xxxv, 7. Grants of mercy call for our returns of duty and the sweet communion we have with God ought ever to be remembered.

It had been called Luz, an almond-tree, but he will have it henceforth called Beth-el, the house of God. This gracious appearance of God to him made it more remarkable than all the almond-trees that flourished there.

glossa.text: « Jacob therefore going forth, » etc. *(GREG., lib. V Moral., c. 11, tom. I.)* To sleep in the way, etc., *as far as* « for the Lord is sweet. »

« He took of the stones, » etc. ((ISID.)) The sleeping of Jacob in the way, the death of Christ on the cross. The stone set under his head is Christ according to his humanity, whom Jacob anointed, that Christ might be signified, for χρίστος in Greek is *anointed* in Latin. But the head is Christ God. The stone therefore set under the head of Jacob signifies the humanity of Christ joined to the God who assumed it. « For the head of the man is Christ, the head of Christ is God ((I Cor. XI.))

« And he saw in his sleep, » etc. ((GREG., Regist. l. I, ep. 24.)) Jacob signifies preachers, who not only, by contemplating, seek after the head of the Church, that is, Christ, but descend by compassion to his members: which the angels ascending and descending show forth. Hence Moses frequently enters the tabernacle, and goes out; and he who within is caught up to contemplation, without is pressed by the business of the weak; within he considers hidden things, without he bears the burdens of the carnal. He who in doubtful matters ever runs back to the tabernacle, consults the Lord before the ark of the testament, giving an example to rulers, that when they are in doubt without as to what they should ordain, they may return to the mind as to a tabernacle, and, as it were before the ark of the testament, may consult the Lord concerning the things they doubt of, seeking within themselves the pages of the sacred eloquence.

*Morally.* To sleep in the way is, in the way of this world, to rest from the hindrance of worldly actions. Jacob sleeping saw angels: because they behold divine things who close their eyes from the desire of temporal things: which, being well closed, the devil opened, saying: « In whatsoever day you shall eat, your eyes shall be opened ((Gen. III)). »

« He saw in his sleep, » etc. ((ISID.)) The angels ascending and descending by the ladder are the evangelists and the preachers of Christ, ascending to the understanding of the Divinity; passing beyond every creature, that they may find in the beginning the Word with God, by whom all things were made. Descending, that they may find him « made of a woman, made under the law, » etc. In that ladder also from earth to heaven, from flesh to spirit: because in it the carnal, by advancing, as it were by ascending, become spiritual. To whom, to be nourished with milk, the spiritual descend, because they cannot speak to them as to spiritual men, but as to carnal. He himself is above in the head, he himself below in his body, that is, the Church; he himself the ladder, who says in John XIV: « I am the way, » etc. To him men ascend, that he may be understood in the heights: and they descend, that he may be nourished in his little members; through him they raise themselves up, that they may look for him on high: and they humble themselves, that they may announce him loftily and with measure.

« I am the Lord God of Abraham, » etc. Mystically it signifies the command of the Divinity directed to the humanity of Christ, to whom the land, that is, the Church, is promised; and to his seed, that is, to the Christian people. Whence psalm II: « Ask of me, and I will give thee the nations for thy inheritance, and the utmost parts of the earth for thy possession. »

« And when he had awaked, » etc. Whosoever shall have awaked after the torpor of sloth, and shall have truly risen up through the exercise of good work, shall understand in the Church the surpassing grace of God and the entrance of the heavenly kingdom.

« Rising therefore, » etc. ((AUG., Q. in Gen., tom. III.)) That Jacob « set up » « the stone which he had put under his head » for a title, and poured oil upon it, he did nothing like to idolatry: because neither then nor afterwards did he frequent the stone by adoring it or by sacrificing to it; but it was a sign and a prophecy pertaining to the anointing, whence Christ is named.

« And he called the name of the city Bethel., » etc. ((HIER., de locis Hebraicis.)) From that which was said, « how terrible is this place, » etc., he imposes on the place the name Bethel, that is, *the house of God,* which before was called Luza, that is, *a nut* or *an almond.* Whence certain men ridiculously think that the Hebrew word *ulam,* is the name of the city: whereas *ulam* is interpreted *before.* This therefore is the order of the reading: He called the name of that place Bethel, and before, Luza was the name of the city. But the ancient writings are full of the word *ulam* or *olam,* which signifies nothing but *before* or *before the porch,* or *a lintel,* or *doorposts,* etc.

notes.text: Afar off — Thou knowest what my thoughts will be in such and such circumstances, long before I know it, yea from all eternity.
Compassest — Thou discernest every step I take. It is a metaphor from soldiers besieging their enemies, and setting watches round about them.
Beset me — With thy all-seeing providence. And laid - Thou keepest me, as it were with a strong hand, in thy sight and under thy power.
I cannot — Apprehend in what manner thou dost so presently know all things.
Hell — If I could hide myself in the lowest parts of the earth.

The wings — If I should flee from east to west: for the sea being the western border of Canaan, is often put for the west in scripture. And wings are poetically ascribed to the morning here, as they are elsewhere to the sun, and to the winds.

glossa.text: *Unto the end, a psalm of David* *Ddvid**.* ((CASS.)) A psalm full of the depth of mysteries, etc., *as far as* veiled in the prophets, manifest in the Gospel. ((AUG.)) The whole Christ speaks, as one entire man, etc., *as far as* as two in one flesh. *Lord, thou hast proved me.* ((CASS.)) First, concerning the knowledge of God, etc., *as far as* fourthly, how the wicked do him no hurt, there, *If thou wilt kill, O God,* etc. *Lord, thou hast proved.* ((AUG.)) Now restored in Jerusalem, etc., *as far as* this is the person of the whole of human nature returning.

*Thou hast understood.* ((CASS.)) The foreknowledge of the Godhead is here shown, etc., *as far as* because the manhood assumed cannot be made equal to the divine substance. *From afar off.* ((AUG.)) While I am still on pilgrimage, before I come to the fatherland, as the father ran to meet the younger son returning, because he understood his thoughts from afar off, because he had said within himself, worn out with want *egestare*: *I will arise and go to my father.*

*My path,* namely the evil one, by which I went, forsaking my father.

*And the line.* (Otherwise) the boundary, how far I came: far indeed had I gone, but thou wast there. He speaks as a fugitive caught, the vengeance of God following after him.

*And all my ways:* before I went in them; and thou didst permit me to go in labour, that I might return if I would not labour: this I confess. *For there is no guile in my tongue:* now I have justified in thy grace.

My *last things,* when I fed the swine, *The old things,* when I asked for the portion of the substance: this according to the parable. But mystically, *The old things,* when through the ancient sin *pecatum* we fell: *The last things,* the penalty, when we came into this mortality, which is the last, if we are willing to return; otherwise the eternal remains. *Thou hast formed me,* unto labours, unto which we are all born. *Thou hast laid.* (Otherwise) Thou hast made heavy the hand, the avenging hand, weighing down the proud man wholesomely, that it may raise up the humble man, in the hand made heavy.

*Wonderful,* and incomprehensible *incomprehensibllis* to me. *Thy knowledge is become.* It is not easy for me to contemplate thee, whom in my pride I forsook, as it was before, when I was with thee, when I said, give me the portion of the substance. *From me,* that is, from my sin.

*It is strengthened,* (otherwise) it has prevailed. *And I shall not be able* to attain to it of myself. ((AUG.)) In Exodus it is read that the Lord, etc., *as far as* I am not hidden from thee, whose boundary thou seest.

*Whither shall I go by thy spirit?* ((CASS.)) The second part, where he now determines that he must not flee *fungiendum* from him, but to him, from him angered to him appeased, which shall be through him with whom the world is full: *For the Spirit of the Lord filleth all things. Whither shall I flee from thy face?* he turns himself this way and that, as though seeking a place of flight.

*If I shall ascend into heaven, thou art there,* etc. ((AUG.)) If I shall lift myself up, I find one to repress me; if I shall be proud of my own justice, *Thou art there,* whose justice it truly is. *If I shall descend,* if by sinning I shall come, *Into hell,* or into the deep, and unwilling to confess: I shall say, who sees me? *Thou art present,* to avenge. He found a counsel, but thus shall I be able to flee from him angered.

*If I shall take wings,* the two wings of charity, which I had lost.

*Wings.* ((CASS.)) Which are of my own power, in *in*; read *id*, "that is" is the efficacy of the Godhead, whereby he raised the body out of the sepulchre. These he took *at daybreak,* before the light, that is, at the time of the resurrection: and *he dwelt in the uttermost parts of the sea,* that is, above the widest end of the world. *And if I shall dwell in the uttermost parts.* ((AUG.)) In mind, at the end of the world, that I may not love the world, but its end, in which there may be rest for me. But he himself also leads thither, whence he subjoins:
*For even there shall thy hand.* But considering the length of the way, he subjoins:

*And he said, perhaps darkness shall tread down,* etc. The iniquity of the world abounds, whereby the wings of charity can grow cold. And because in the night I despaired of crossing the sea, the night was made a light to me: There came a woman, the wisdom of God, who had lost the groat wherein is the image of the king, that is, man: she lighted from herself a lamp, which is of clay, that is, flesh, and the night being lit up she found the groat.

*And he said.* ((AUG.)) I deliberated.

*Perhaps thee.* By darkness he means that lower part of the rational creature, pressing upon him as an adversary, namely wicked men or the flesh, whence he fears: And it is, *Darkness,* that is, the lower rational creature holding the left-hand way.

*They have trodden me down.* ((ID.)) So I feared, but *the night was made a light, in my delights,* that is, to those who, being before night, shall be enlightened in delights. *Because thee.* Sinners.

*They shall not be darkened,* etc., *and the night,* by the sinners that dwell there. *As the day,* that is, the saints out of the Jews. *As his darkness, so also his light,* because in so far as he acknowledges, in so far he pardons. But whence is this to me? *because thou hast possessed my reins. Because darkness.* ((AUG.)) He who confesses not his sins darkens his own darkness; but if he confesses, God enlightens. *As his darkness.* Of our night, that is, the miseries of human life, etc., *as far as* whom the light does not lift up.

notes.text: We are not debtors to the flesh — We ought not to follow it.

The deeds of the flesh — Not only evil actions, but evil desires, tempers, thoughts. If ye mortify - Kill, destroy these. Ye shall live - The life of faith more abundantly here, and hereafter the life of glory.

For as many as are led by the Spirit of God — In all the ways of righteousness. They are the sons of God - Here St. Paul enters upon the description of those blessings which he comprises, ver. 30, in the word glorified; though, indeed, he does not describe mere glory, but that which is still mingled with the cross. The sum is, through sufferings to glory.

For ye — Who are real Christians. Have not received the spirit of bondage - The Holy Ghost was not properly a spirit of bondage, even in the time of the Old Testament. Yet there was something of bondage remaining even in those who then had received the Spirit. Again - As the Jews did before. We - All and every believer. Cry - The word denotes a vehement speaking, with desire, confidence, constancy. Abba, Father - The latter word explains the former. By using both the Syriac and the Greek word, St. Paul seems to point out the joint cry both of the Jewish and gentile believers. The spirit of bondage here seems directly to mean, those operations of the Holy Spirit by which the soul, on its first conviction, feels itself in bondage to sin, to the world, to Satan, and obnoxious to the wrath of God. This, therefore, and the Spirit of adoption, are one and the same Spirit, only manifesting itself in various operations, according to the various circumstances of the persons.

The same Spirit beareth witness with our spirit — With the spirit of every true believer, by a testimony distinct from that of his own spirit, or the testimony of a good conscience. Happy they who enjoy this clear and constant.

Joint heirs — That we may know it is a great inheritance which God will give us for he hath given a great one to his Son. If we suffer with him - Willingly and cheerfully, for righteousness' sake. This is a new proposition, referring to what follows.
For I reckon — This verse gives the reason why he but now mentioned sufferings and glory. When that glory "shall be revealed in us," then the sons of God will be revealed also.

For the earnest expectation — The word denotes a lively hope of something drawing near, and a vehement longing after it. Of the creation - Of all visible creatures, believers excepted, who are spoken of apart; each kind, according as it is capable. All these have been sufferers through sin; and to all these (the finally impenitent excepted) shall refreshment redound from the glory of the children of God. Upright heathens are by no means to be excluded from this earnest expectation: nay, perhaps something of it may at some times be found even in the vainest of men; who (although in the hurry of life they mistake vanity for liberty, and partly stifle, partly dissemble, their groans, yet) in their sober, quiet, sleepless, afflicted hours, pour forth many sighs in the ear of God.

The creation was made subject to vanity — Abuse, misery, and corruption. By him who subjected it - Namely, God, Gen. iii, 17, v, 29. Adam only made it liable to the sentence which God pronounced; yet not without hope.

The creation itself shall be delivered — Destruction is not deliverance: therefore whatsoever is destroyed, or ceases to be, is not delivered at all. Will, then, any part of the creation be destroyed? Into the glorious liberty - The excellent state wherein they were created.

For the whole creation groaneth together — With joint groans, as it were with one voice. And travaileth - Literally, is in the pains of childbirth, to be delivered of the burden of the curse. Until now - To this very hour; and so on till the time of deliverance.

And even we, who have the first-fruits of the Spirit — That is, the Spirit, who is the first-fruits of our inheritance. The adoption - Persons who had been privately adopted among the Roman were often brought forth into the forum, and there publicly owned as their sons by those who adopted them. So at the general resurrection, when the body itself is redeemed from death, the sons of God shall be publicly owned by him in the great assembly of men and angels. The redemption of our body - From corruption to glory and immortality.
For we are saved by hope — Our salvation is now only in hope. We do not yet possess this full salvation.

glossa.text: *But if by the Spirit.* Either by the Holy Spirit or by our own: which nevertheless is not so, save by the working of the Holy Spirit.

*They are driven.* He says they are driven, not they are ruled. For it is more to be driven than to be ruled: for we say that one is driven, as scarcely doing anything; but that he is ruled, as already doing something, who is therefore ruled that he may act rightly. But they are driven, not because they do nothing of themselves, but because, that they may do something, they are impelled by the force of grace.

((AUG., lib. de Correp. et Grat., c. 2.)) Let them not therefore deceive themselves who say: To what end for us, etc., *as far as* let them rejoice that they have received.

*For you have not received,* etc. You ought to be sons, not servants, because you have not received the spirit of bondage: which makes men serve unwilling through fear of punishment.

*But you have received the spirit of adoption.* It is the same spirit, but because of diverse works it is differently named: he is called the spirit of wrath to the Egyptians, to whom the water divided by the spirit did harm. The son of Israel is not called [a spirit] of wrath, to whom the divided water was of profit. He is the spirit of fear to those who, convicted by the law of their sins and of their own weakness, did not understand the grace of the spirit. He is the spirit of liberty by his working to those to whom regeneration unto life eternal, and faith which works through love, has been imparted. One spirit therefore, which makes two fears. Which also make two kinds of servants. For there is a servant who is also a son, who fears the Lord and honours the father, whence Malachi: *If I am Lord, where is my fear? If father, where is my honour? ((Malach. I))*. And there is a servant who fears punishment, but does not love justice. And because mention is made of fears, it is to be known that besides the natural fear, which is in all, there are four fears, namely: the worldly, which is evil and not from God; and the servile, which is good and from God, but is not sufficient; the initial, which is good and sufficient; and the chaste, which is good and perfecting, of which it is here treated: *For it begets us sons of God. In whom we cry.* This again is from the gift of the Spirit, which makes us so to cry *Abba,* in Hebrew, *father* in Latin. *Abba, father.* Because of the mystery, the Apostle set down both. And in his passion Christ said, *Abba, father,* because the Church is of both peoples, and suffering with her he showed in himself that her sons (the martyrs, namely) ought not to despair, if at the time of passion any sadness from human frailty should creep in.

*That we are the sons of God.* This the Holy Spirit makes us to recognize, while in the Church remission of sins is made; which although the whole Trinity works, yet it is understood to pertain to the Holy Spirit, because he is common to the Father and the Son, and the union of both; through whom is made that fellowship and unity by which we are made one body of the only-begotten Son of God. For unity joins us together, which charity makes, which is not save from the Holy Spirit. These things are said that we may love unity, and fear separation.

*Heirs.* Even though God does not depart, which is spoken according to human laws. Or he will depart, so that he be not seen through a glass in a dark manner as now, but face to face. It can also be said that Christ our head, departing to the passion, left us the possession of ecclesiastical peace, as he himself says: *My peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you ((Joan. XIV))*. Christ also is our inheritance. Whence: *The Lord is the portion of my inheritance ((Psal. XV))*, etc.

*If yet we suffer with him.* To mortify the deeds of the flesh, whence life shall be, no one can without trouble, for which patience is necessary.

*For the expectation of the creature.* The creature: they are the good, who remain in the creation of God, or because they are the cause of all things. Corruption is vanity, to which the creature is subjected. For all things that are born are weak and corruptible, and thereby vain: because they cannot keep their own state.

((AUG.)) What he says, *for the expectation,* etc. It is so to be understood that neither sense, etc., *as far as* it labours and lies under corruption.

*Not willingly,* etc. Willingly it sinned, but not willingly does it bear the penalty, in that it is subjected to deceit: but because of the justice and the clemency of him who both punishes sin, and purposes to heal.

*Because the creature itself also. ((AUG.))* Now it is a creature only, since the form of the sons is not yet perfected, etc., *as far as* for man, having lost the seal of the image, remained only a creature.

*Shall be delivered.* He shall be revealed; it awaits *revela*; he subjoined, shall be delivered. All these things through the Spirit.

*Every creature. ((AUG.))* Man. Every creature is either corporeal, etc., *as far as* although not in all men. *Every creature. ((AMBR.))* All the elements fulfil their offices with labour, which is for our sake: whence they shall rest when we have been taken up; and therefore let us prepare ourselves diligently.

*It groaneth.* It is always new in this, which is marked by the inchoative verb, and for desire of the heavenly fatherland. *It travaileth.* That is, it grieves.

*Until now. ((AUG.))* Because although some one in Abraham's bosom has ceased to grieve, yet still in those who are not yet delivered every creature groans.

*Not only,* etc. ((AUG.)) That is, not only in the man of the body, but we also in our own selves apart from the body, the troubles of the body excepted.

*Not only. ((AUG., in expos. propos. in 53. in epist. ad Rom.))* Not only that which in men is called merely a creature, etc., *as far as* or with trouble disquieting.

 *The first-fruits of the spirit.* That is, of those whose spirits have already been offered to God as in sacrifice, and kindled with the divine fire of charity. *Adoption.* That the body also may receive the benefit of adoption, and that in every part they may be sons of God.

*For by hope.* He therefore says it that the merit of hope may seem the greater and therefore ought to save.

*The Spirit helpeth our infirmity. ((AUG.))* Because we groan and ask to be delivered, but lest we ask either before the time or contrariwise, the Spirit helps. What prayer obtains is evidently the gift of God, but to pray also is of grace.

notes.text: He proposed another parable — in which he farther explains the case of unfruitful hearers. The kingdom of heaven (as has been observed before) sometimes signifies eternal glory: sometimes the way to it, inward religion; sometimes, as here, the Gospel dispensation: the phrase is likewise used for a person or thing relating to any one of those: so in this place it means, Christ preaching the Gospel, who is like a man sowing good seed - The expression, is like, both here and in several other places, only means, that the thing spoken of may be illustrated by the following similitude. Who sowed good seed in his field - God sowed nothing but good in his whole creation. Christ sowed only the good seed of truth in his Church.

But while men slept — They ought to have watched: the Lord of the field sleepeth not. His enemy came and sowed darnel - This is very like wheat, and commonly grows among wheat rather than among other grain: but tares or vetches are of the pulse kind, and bear no resemblance to wheat.
When the blade was sprung up, then appeared the darnel — It was not discerned before: it seldom appears, as soon as the good seed is sown: all at first appears to be peace, and love, and joy.

Didst not thou sow good seed in thy field? Whence then hath it darnel? — Not from the parent of good. Even the heathen could say, "No evil can from thee proceed: 'Tis only suffer'd, not decreed: As darkness is not from the sun, Nor mount the shades, till he is gone."

He said, An enemy hath done this — A plain answer to the great question concerning the origin of evil. God made men (as he did angels) intelligent creatures, and consequently free either to choose good or evil: but he implanted no evil in the human soul: An enemy (with man's concurrence) hath done this. Darnel, in the Church, is properly outside Christians, such as have the form of godliness, without the power. Open sinners, such as have neither the form nor the power, are not so properly darnel, as thistles and brambles: these ought to be rooted up without delay, and not suffered in the Christian community. Whereas should fallible men attempt to gather up the darnel, they would often root up the wheat with them.

glossa.text: *Another parable.* As a rich householder refreshes those he has invited with diverse foods, that each one might take various nourishments according to the nature of his own stomach. Whence he also said another parable and not the other, that more may be understood to follow. This parable is set forth, and, the crowds being dismissed, it is expounded at home to the disciples who ask. And here he teaches good will, and caution, and patience, and discretion, and long-suffering, and justice.
*Men.* Those who are appointed over others in the Church for their protection and keeping: or when the apostles shall receive the sleep of death.

*Wilt thou that we go.* When a spiritual man hears that this is from the devil, who avails nothing against the will of God, a will may arise in him to take such men out of the world, if he should have the power. But he consults the justice of God, whether he ought to do it, and whether God wills this to be the office of men. But the Truth answers: that a man does not know in this life what he will be who now errs, and what his error confers upon the good: and that they are therefore not to be taken away, lest perhaps they be slain who perhaps are yet to be [good]: or lest it hurt the good, to whom they are profitable, etc. But that this is then done seasonably, when there is no longer a time for changing one's life and for profiting others: and then, he says, it is done not by men, but by angels.

*And he said: No,* etc. Behold patience. For he did not blaze out into anger when the grievance was heard, nor did he wish to avenge himself at once; so let us also, when injured, bear it patiently.

*Lest perhaps.* Here place is given to repentance, and we are admonished not to cut off quickly: because he who errs today will perhaps tomorrow defend the truth. If therefore he were plucked up now, the wheat that was to be would be rooted out. Or it is necessary that the evil be mingled with the good, by whom they may be exercised. Or by comparison with whom they may strive toward what is better; and when these are taken away, the height of charity withers, which is to be rooted out.

There the evil are to be borne patiently, where some are found by whom the good are helped.

((AUG.)) A multitude is not to be excommunicated, nor the prince of the people.

*Suffer.* This seems contrary to that word of the Apostle: *Put away the evil one from among you ((I Cor. V))*. But as between the cockle and the wheat, so long as it is in the blade, there is little difference: so the Lord admonishes us not to judge concerning a doubtful thing, which the Lord in the day of judgment will condemn not by suspicion, but manifestly.

In suffering let us meditate justice: in judging let us not neglect justice.

*And in the time.* He who has borne long-sufferingly, by justice repays what is deserved: for the virtues are distinct, but not contrary. *And bind ye.* In this life there is no binding, otherwise so many would not come to their senses out of error.

notes.text: Truth — In the way of thy precepts, which are true and right in all things. My heart - Knit my whole heart to thyself.

Hell — From extreme dangers and miseries. This psalm contains a commendation of Zion, a type of the gospel-church, which is here preferred before the rest of the land of Canaan, ver. 1, 2, 3. And before any other place, as being filled with more eminent men, and more of divine blessings, ver. 4-7. A psalm or song for the sons of Korah.

glossa.text: *Conduct me, O Lord, in thy way.* ((CASS.)) He prays for all who now adore, and speaks in his members. *O Lord, conduct,* etc. It is one thing to be led to the way, and another to be led in the way, lest one fall in it: everywhere men need to be helped, whether they be in the way, or outside it. But the way is Christ, who says: *I am the way, the truth, and the life. Let my heart rejoice.* ((AUG.)) In worldly fear the cause goes before, etc., *as far as* but he who fears, and does not hope, is cast down.
*From the lower hell.* ((ID.)) By this we understand, etc., *as far as* these are opinions, not assertions.

*O God, the wicked have risen up against me, and the Synagogue of the mighty,* etc. ((CASS.)) Again he prays for himself, mention being made of his passion and of his glory, whence those for whom he prayed have much mercy and are rescued from hell.

*Give thy command.* ((AUG.)) As if he should say: Let the time of patience pass, let the time of judgment come, whence not only Christ, but the saints also, shall sit as judges, who are *the sons of the handmaid,* that is, of the Church.

notes.text: We are not debtors to the flesh — We ought not to follow it.

The deeds of the flesh — Not only evil actions, but evil desires, tempers, thoughts. If ye mortify - Kill, destroy these. Ye shall live - The life of faith more abundantly here, and hereafter the life of glory.

For as many as are led by the Spirit of God — In all the ways of righteousness. They are the sons of God - Here St. Paul enters upon the description of those blessings which he comprises, ver. 30, in the word glorified; though, indeed, he does not describe mere glory, but that which is still mingled with the cross. The sum is, through sufferings to glory.

For ye — Who are real Christians. Have not received the spirit of bondage - The Holy Ghost was not properly a spirit of bondage, even in the time of the Old Testament. Yet there was something of bondage remaining even in those who then had received the Spirit. Again - As the Jews did before. We - All and every believer. Cry - The word denotes a vehement speaking, with desire, confidence, constancy. Abba, Father - The latter word explains the former. By using both the Syriac and the Greek word, St. Paul seems to point out the joint cry both of the Jewish and gentile believers. The spirit of bondage here seems directly to mean, those operations of the Holy Spirit by which the soul, on its first conviction, feels itself in bondage to sin, to the world, to Satan, and obnoxious to the wrath of God. This, therefore, and the Spirit of adoption, are one and the same Spirit, only manifesting itself in various operations, according to the various circumstances of the persons.

The same Spirit beareth witness with our spirit — With the spirit of every true believer, by a testimony distinct from that of his own spirit, or the testimony of a good conscience. Happy they who enjoy this clear and constant.

Joint heirs — That we may know it is a great inheritance which God will give us for he hath given a great one to his Son. If we suffer with him - Willingly and cheerfully, for righteousness' sake. This is a new proposition, referring to what follows.
For I reckon — This verse gives the reason why he but now mentioned sufferings and glory. When that glory "shall be revealed in us," then the sons of God will be revealed also.

For the earnest expectation — The word denotes a lively hope of something drawing near, and a vehement longing after it. Of the creation - Of all visible creatures, believers excepted, who are spoken of apart; each kind, according as it is capable. All these have been sufferers through sin; and to all these (the finally impenitent excepted) shall refreshment redound from the glory of the children of God. Upright heathens are by no means to be excluded from this earnest expectation: nay, perhaps something of it may at some times be found even in the vainest of men; who (although in the hurry of life they mistake vanity for liberty, and partly stifle, partly dissemble, their groans, yet) in their sober, quiet, sleepless, afflicted hours, pour forth many sighs in the ear of God.

The creation was made subject to vanity — Abuse, misery, and corruption. By him who subjected it - Namely, God, Gen. iii, 17, v, 29. Adam only made it liable to the sentence which God pronounced; yet not without hope.

The creation itself shall be delivered — Destruction is not deliverance: therefore whatsoever is destroyed, or ceases to be, is not delivered at all. Will, then, any part of the creation be destroyed? Into the glorious liberty - The excellent state wherein they were created.

For the whole creation groaneth together — With joint groans, as it were with one voice. And travaileth - Literally, is in the pains of childbirth, to be delivered of the burden of the curse. Until now - To this very hour; and so on till the time of deliverance.

And even we, who have the first-fruits of the Spirit — That is, the Spirit, who is the first-fruits of our inheritance. The adoption - Persons who had been privately adopted among the Roman were often brought forth into the forum, and there publicly owned as their sons by those who adopted them. So at the general resurrection, when the body itself is redeemed from death, the sons of God shall be publicly owned by him in the great assembly of men and angels. The redemption of our body - From corruption to glory and immortality.
For we are saved by hope — Our salvation is now only in hope. We do not yet possess this full salvation.

glossa.text: *But if by the Spirit.* Either by the Holy Spirit or by our own: which nevertheless is not so, save by the working of the Holy Spirit.

*They are driven.* He says they are driven, not they are ruled. For it is more to be driven than to be ruled: for we say that one is driven, as scarcely doing anything; but that he is ruled, as already doing something, who is therefore ruled that he may act rightly. But they are driven, not because they do nothing of themselves, but because, that they may do something, they are impelled by the force of grace.

((AUG., lib. de Correp. et Grat., c. 2.)) Let them not therefore deceive themselves who say: To what end for us, etc., *as far as* let them rejoice that they have received.

*For you have not received,* etc. You ought to be sons, not servants, because you have not received the spirit of bondage: which makes men serve unwilling through fear of punishment.

*But you have received the spirit of adoption.* It is the same spirit, but because of diverse works it is differently named: he is called the spirit of wrath to the Egyptians, to whom the water divided by the spirit did harm. The son of Israel is not called [a spirit] of wrath, to whom the divided water was of profit. He is the spirit of fear to those who, convicted by the law of their sins and of their own weakness, did not understand the grace of the spirit. He is the spirit of liberty by his working to those to whom regeneration unto life eternal, and faith which works through love, has been imparted. One spirit therefore, which makes two fears. Which also make two kinds of servants. For there is a servant who is also a son, who fears the Lord and honours the father, whence Malachi: *If I am Lord, where is my fear? If father, where is my honour? ((Malach. I))*. And there is a servant who fears punishment, but does not love justice. And because mention is made of fears, it is to be known that besides the natural fear, which is in all, there are four fears, namely: the worldly, which is evil and not from God; and the servile, which is good and from God, but is not sufficient; the initial, which is good and sufficient; and the chaste, which is good and perfecting, of which it is here treated: *For it begets us sons of God. In whom we cry.* This again is from the gift of the Spirit, which makes us so to cry *Abba,* in Hebrew, *father* in Latin. *Abba, father.* Because of the mystery, the Apostle set down both. And in his passion Christ said, *Abba, father,* because the Church is of both peoples, and suffering with her he showed in himself that her sons (the martyrs, namely) ought not to despair, if at the time of passion any sadness from human frailty should creep in.

*That we are the sons of God.* This the Holy Spirit makes us to recognize, while in the Church remission of sins is made; which although the whole Trinity works, yet it is understood to pertain to the Holy Spirit, because he is common to the Father and the Son, and the union of both; through whom is made that fellowship and unity by which we are made one body of the only-begotten Son of God. For unity joins us together, which charity makes, which is not save from the Holy Spirit. These things are said that we may love unity, and fear separation.

*Heirs.* Even though God does not depart, which is spoken according to human laws. Or he will depart, so that he be not seen through a glass in a dark manner as now, but face to face. It can also be said that Christ our head, departing to the passion, left us the possession of ecclesiastical peace, as he himself says: *My peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you ((Joan. XIV))*. Christ also is our inheritance. Whence: *The Lord is the portion of my inheritance ((Psal. XV))*, etc.

*If yet we suffer with him.* To mortify the deeds of the flesh, whence life shall be, no one can without trouble, for which patience is necessary.

*For the expectation of the creature.* The creature: they are the good, who remain in the creation of God, or because they are the cause of all things. Corruption is vanity, to which the creature is subjected. For all things that are born are weak and corruptible, and thereby vain: because they cannot keep their own state.

((AUG.)) What he says, *for the expectation,* etc. It is so to be understood that neither sense, etc., *as far as* it labours and lies under corruption.

*Not willingly,* etc. Willingly it sinned, but not willingly does it bear the penalty, in that it is subjected to deceit: but because of the justice and the clemency of him who both punishes sin, and purposes to heal.

*Because the creature itself also. ((AUG.))* Now it is a creature only, since the form of the sons is not yet perfected, etc., *as far as* for man, having lost the seal of the image, remained only a creature.

*Shall be delivered.* He shall be revealed; it awaits *revela*; he subjoined, shall be delivered. All these things through the Spirit.

*Every creature. ((AUG.))* Man. Every creature is either corporeal, etc., *as far as* although not in all men. *Every creature. ((AMBR.))* All the elements fulfil their offices with labour, which is for our sake: whence they shall rest when we have been taken up; and therefore let us prepare ourselves diligently.

*It groaneth.* It is always new in this, which is marked by the inchoative verb, and for desire of the heavenly fatherland. *It travaileth.* That is, it grieves.

*Until now. ((AUG.))* Because although some one in Abraham's bosom has ceased to grieve, yet still in those who are not yet delivered every creature groans.

*Not only,* etc. ((AUG.)) That is, not only in the man of the body, but we also in our own selves apart from the body, the troubles of the body excepted.

*Not only. ((AUG., in expos. propos. in 53. in epist. ad Rom.))* Not only that which in men is called merely a creature, etc., *as far as* or with trouble disquieting.

 *The first-fruits of the spirit.* That is, of those whose spirits have already been offered to God as in sacrifice, and kindled with the divine fire of charity. *Adoption.* That the body also may receive the benefit of adoption, and that in every part they may be sons of God.

*For by hope.* He therefore says it that the merit of hope may seem the greater and therefore ought to save.

*The Spirit helpeth our infirmity. ((AUG.))* Because we groan and ask to be delivered, but lest we ask either before the time or contrariwise, the Spirit helps. What prayer obtains is evidently the gift of God, but to pray also is of grace.

notes.text: He proposed another parable — in which he farther explains the case of unfruitful hearers. The kingdom of heaven (as has been observed before) sometimes signifies eternal glory: sometimes the way to it, inward religion; sometimes, as here, the Gospel dispensation: the phrase is likewise used for a person or thing relating to any one of those: so in this place it means, Christ preaching the Gospel, who is like a man sowing good seed - The expression, is like, both here and in several other places, only means, that the thing spoken of may be illustrated by the following similitude. Who sowed good seed in his field - God sowed nothing but good in his whole creation. Christ sowed only the good seed of truth in his Church.

But while men slept — They ought to have watched: the Lord of the field sleepeth not. His enemy came and sowed darnel - This is very like wheat, and commonly grows among wheat rather than among other grain: but tares or vetches are of the pulse kind, and bear no resemblance to wheat.
When the blade was sprung up, then appeared the darnel — It was not discerned before: it seldom appears, as soon as the good seed is sown: all at first appears to be peace, and love, and joy.

Didst not thou sow good seed in thy field? Whence then hath it darnel? — Not from the parent of good. Even the heathen could say, "No evil can from thee proceed: 'Tis only suffer'd, not decreed: As darkness is not from the sun, Nor mount the shades, till he is gone."

He said, An enemy hath done this — A plain answer to the great question concerning the origin of evil. God made men (as he did angels) intelligent creatures, and consequently free either to choose good or evil: but he implanted no evil in the human soul: An enemy (with man's concurrence) hath done this. Darnel, in the Church, is properly outside Christians, such as have the form of godliness, without the power. Open sinners, such as have neither the form nor the power, are not so properly darnel, as thistles and brambles: these ought to be rooted up without delay, and not suffered in the Christian community. Whereas should fallible men attempt to gather up the darnel, they would often root up the wheat with them.

glossa.text: *Another parable.* As a rich householder refreshes those he has invited with diverse foods, that each one might take various nourishments according to the nature of his own stomach. Whence he also said another parable and not the other, that more may be understood to follow. This parable is set forth, and, the crowds being dismissed, it is expounded at home to the disciples who ask. And here he teaches good will, and caution, and patience, and discretion, and long-suffering, and justice.
*Men.* Those who are appointed over others in the Church for their protection and keeping: or when the apostles shall receive the sleep of death.

*Wilt thou that we go.* When a spiritual man hears that this is from the devil, who avails nothing against the will of God, a will may arise in him to take such men out of the world, if he should have the power. But he consults the justice of God, whether he ought to do it, and whether God wills this to be the office of men. But the Truth answers: that a man does not know in this life what he will be who now errs, and what his error confers upon the good: and that they are therefore not to be taken away, lest perhaps they be slain who perhaps are yet to be [good]: or lest it hurt the good, to whom they are profitable, etc. But that this is then done seasonably, when there is no longer a time for changing one's life and for profiting others: and then, he says, it is done not by men, but by angels.

*And he said: No,* etc. Behold patience. For he did not blaze out into anger when the grievance was heard, nor did he wish to avenge himself at once; so let us also, when injured, bear it patiently.

*Lest perhaps.* Here place is given to repentance, and we are admonished not to cut off quickly: because he who errs today will perhaps tomorrow defend the truth. If therefore he were plucked up now, the wheat that was to be would be rooted out. Or it is necessary that the evil be mingled with the good, by whom they may be exercised. Or by comparison with whom they may strive toward what is better; and when these are taken away, the height of charity withers, which is to be rooted out.

There the evil are to be borne patiently, where some are found by whom the good are helped.

((AUG.)) A multitude is not to be excommunicated, nor the prince of the people.

*Suffer.* This seems contrary to that word of the Apostle: *Put away the evil one from among you ((I Cor. V))*. But as between the cockle and the wheat, so long as it is in the blade, there is little difference: so the Lord admonishes us not to judge concerning a doubtful thing, which the Lord in the day of judgment will condemn not by suspicion, but manifestly.

In suffering let us meditate justice: in judging let us not neglect justice.

*And in the time.* He who has borne long-sufferingly, by justice repays what is deserved: for the virtues are distinct, but not contrary. *And bind ye.* In this life there is no binding, otherwise so many would not come to their senses out of error.

lines: Jacob lay down on a stone and dreamed of a ladder.
Surely the Lord is in this place.
Where can we go from your Spirit, where flee from your face?
If we make our bed in the dark, you are there.
You searched us out before we said a word.
You have known us all along.
Come, let us worship the God who is here.
This is the house of God. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Feel the hard stone Jacob put under his head in the empty country, alone, on the run, with nowhere left to go.
Surely the Lord is in this place.
And in the night a stairway opened from earth to heaven, angels going up and down, and a voice promising: I am with you.
Surely the Lord is in this place.
The psalmist says it too — there is no dark you can crawl into where God is not already waiting.
Surely the Lord is in this place.
You were searched and known before you walked through that door, and the God who knows you is glad you came.
Surely the Lord is in this place. This is the gate of heaven!

turn.gravity: Wisdom says God judges with mildness and great forbearance, and so teaches his people that the righteous must be kind; Paul hears the whole creation groaning in hope; and Jesus tells of a field where wheat and weeds grow tangled until harvest. The nerve: how to live faithfully in a world — and a church — that will not sort cleanly into good and evil.
turn.trap: The parable gets read as a shrug ("don't judge anything") or, flipped, as a mandate for the zealous to start pulling weeds — purging the church, the family, the world of the wrong people. Both miss that the restraint is the King's command and the sorting is the King's alone.
turn.hinge: The weeds are real — the enemy's own work, not to be pretended away — and you are forbidden to pull them, because your hands cannot tell wheat from weed without tearing up both. Real evil, real judgment, and your task in the meantime is patience, not harvest.

doors.claim: You are not the reaper — pulling the weeds now would tear up wheat with them, so the command is a hard patience that leaves room for the weed to become wheat.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: Room for repentance is left, and we are warned not to cut off a brother hastily, since one who today is corrupted by error may tomorrow be set right.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: This the Lord spoke to forbid any putting to death; for we ought not to kill even a heretic, since so a never-ending war would be brought into the world.

doors.say: Your hands are not steady enough to weed God's field; the patience that galls you is mercy leaving a door open.
doors.do: Name one person they have already written off as a weed, and ask them to keep the door of repentance open instead of uprooting.

doors.claim: The weeds came in the unguarded hour, sown by an enemy and not by God — which both names the origin of evil and calls the sleepers to wake.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: "While men slept" — while the leaders of the Church lay in supineness, and after the Apostles had fallen into the sleep of death, then the enemy came.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: While men slept — they ought to have watched; the Lord of the field never sleeps. An enemy has done this: a plain answer to the great question of the origin of evil.

doors.say: The weeds in your life and your church are not from the hand of God — they were sown in a sleeping hour, and the call is to wake.
doors.do: Point to one unguarded place — a habit, a relationship, a corner of the church — where vigilance has lapsed, and watch there again.

doors.claim: The mixed field is not the last word — there is a harvest, a real and final sorting that belongs to God, where the weeds are bound and the righteous shine like the sun.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: Behold the love of God: ready to show mercy, slow to punish. When he sows, he sows himself; when he punishes, he punishes by others — by the angels.

witnesses.author: Remigius of Auxerre
witnesses.reading: The harvest is the day of judgment, when the good are parted from the evil by the ministry of angels; the righteous, who now shine for an example, shall then shine as the sun.

doors.say: Leave the verdict to the harvest — it is coming, it is God's, and the wheat will shine in it.
doors.do: Turn anxious or vengeful hearts from rendering verdicts now to entrusting the harvest to God — and to living as wheat.

synthesis.convergence: The readings show a sovereignty that looks like forbearance — a God who judges with mildness and teaches his people to be kind (Wisdom 12), who abounds in steadfast love (Psalm 86), who waits with a groaning creation that hopes for what it cannot yet see (Romans 8) — over a field where wheat and weeds grow tangled until harvest.
synthesis.claim: The God who could uproot every weed chooses patience and kindness instead — and asks the same costly patience of you.
synthesis.here: For people quick to sort the world (and the church) into the righteous and the villains, the move is the hard patience of hope: leave the harvest to God, extend to the 'weeds' the mildness God extends to you, and wait — with the whole groaning creation — for a verdict that is not yours to render.

turn.subtract: Three doors, three landings — patience (let both grow), vigilance (while they slept), hope-and-warning (the harvest sorts it). Choose one for your people and let the others go.
turn.source: Catena Aurea (Aquinas; J.H. Newman tr., public domain) + Wesley's Explanatory Notes, retrieved from ~/reception-corpus — attested, not authored.
